title: Designing view transitions

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Use the vercel-react-view-transitions skill

events.content:
All changes build cleanly. Here's a summary of what was implemented:

### Files changed

**`app/NavigationEvents.tsx`** (new) — Client component that:
- Intercepts `<a>` clicks in capture phase to set direction to `forward`
- Monkey-patches `router.push`/`router.replace` to wrap navigation in `document.startViewTransition()`
- Uses `MutationObserver` + double `requestAnimationFrame` to wait for DOM commit before capturing the new snapshot for the transition
- Sets `data-nav-direction` on `<html>` for CSS to read, defaults to `back`

**`app/globals.css`** — Added:
- **Page slide transitions**: `html[data-nav-direction="forward"]::view-transition-old/new(root)` slides old left/new from right (forward). Default `::view-transition-old/new(root)` slides old right/new from left (back)
- **Shared element morphing**: `::view-transition-group(*)` at 400ms ease-in-out — the product image `view-transition-name` causes the browser to interpolate position/size/border-radius between the grid thumbnail and detail hero
- **Suspense content fade-ins**: `.suspense-content-enter` (fade + slide up) and `.suspense-grid-enter` (fade) animate in when content replaces skeletons
- **`prefers-reduced-motion`** media query: zeros out all animation/transition durations on everything including view transition pseudo-elements

**`app/ProductGrid.tsx`** — Added `viewTransitionName: 'product-image-${slug}'` inline style on each `.product-image` div, plus `suspense-grid-enter` class on the grid container

**`app/product/[slug]/page.tsx`** — Added `viewTransitionName: 'product-image-${slug}'` on the `.product-hero` div (matching the grid thumbnail name), and `suspense-content-enter` class on resolved `ProductDetails`

**`app/layout.tsx`** — Renders `<NavigationEvents />`

**`next.config.ts`** — Stripped experimental flags (not needed; everything is handled client-side)
